title: 100 million photons per second from a single organic molecule
authors: Siwei Luo, Tim Hebenstreit, Alexey Shkarin, Jan Renger, Tobias Utikal, Stephan Goetzinger
abstract: At cryogenic temperatures, organic single-photon sources (SPSs) offer Fourier-limited emission, virtually unlimited photostability, and emission wavelengths selectable by molecular design, making them attractive for quantum metrology, secure communication, and photonic quantum information processing. However, their efficient integration with photonic microstructures has remained challenging, limiting photon collection from single organic emitters under cryogenic operation. Here, we demonstrate a cryogenic planar metallo-dielectric antenna that efficiently directs the emission of a single dibenzoterrylene (DBT) molecule towards the collection optics. The device reaches a collection efficiency of 97% and delivers 100 million photons per second into the first lens. We measure a photon indistinguishability for the Fourier-limited transition of 91.2% while maintaining a high single-photon purity of 97.7% under strong continuous-wave (CW) and pulsed excitation. These results establish organic molecules as a high-performance platform for single-photon generation and represent an important step towards scalable organic quantum photonic technologies.
summary: The research demonstrates a novel, high-efficiency antenna structure that successfully couples single photons from organic molecules (DBT) into an optical fiber. By overcoming previous photon collection limitations, the system achieves high brightness, high purity, and near-unity indistinguishability, establishing organic molecules as a viable platform for quantum photonics.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is efficiently collecting single photons emitted from organic single-photon sources (SPSs) embedded in crystals under cryogenic conditions.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a planar metallo-dielectric antenna that achieves a high collection efficiency of 97% and generates photons at a rate of 100 million per second with high indistinguishability (91.2%).
method: The study involves fabricating and characterizing a specialized antenna structure coupled to an organic emitter (DBT) and measuring photon properties using cryogenic spectroscopy and Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry.
model_or_system: The system uses a single dibenzoterrylene (DBT) molecule embedded in a p-DCB crystal, coupled to a custom-designed cryogenic planar metallo-dielectric antenna structure. This antenna acts as a quasi-waveguide to enhance photon extraction.
key_observables: Collection efficiency ($\approx 97\%$), photon rate ($\sim 10^8$ photons/s), single-photon purity ($>97.7\%$), and photon indistinguishability ($91.2\%$).
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperatures (below 2 K), high photon flux (Mcps regime), and the molecular transition properties of DBT.
main_assumptions: The antenna design is assumed to effectively direct emission without requiring complex micro/nanostructuring of the host crystal, although residual dephasing was identified as a limitation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic, microscope image, and cross-section of the metallo-dielectric antenna structure, detailing its layered geometry.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the limitations of organic SPSs, then presenting the antenna design as a solution, followed by detailed measurements of collection efficiency, purity, and indistinguishability under both CW and pulsed excitation regimes.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of coupling molecular quantum emitters to photonic circuits, which is crucial for scaling up quantum photonic devices and quantum networks.
